missing: S7 ('A content-only edit six months later requires no dev server,' measured via Content mode §15.5) is listed as an unconditional whole-product success criterion, but §3.3's usage-model table tags the underlying 'Content edit' mode as '(v2)' — a feature not delivered in v1. Nothing on S7 flags this dependency or version-gates the criterion.
why_it_matters: A reader trying to certify 'all success criteria met' for a v1 ship has no way to pass S7, because the capability it measures does not exist yet in v1. This is the same class of unconditioned-acceptance-criterion problem already flagged for §19/O6 elsewhere in the PRD, but this instance (§2.3 vs §3.3) is new and unrecorded.
suggested_fix: Either add a version qualifier to S7 ('v2 criterion') and remove it from the v1 success bar, or pull Content mode into v1 scope so the top-level criterion is actually achievable at ship.

missing: G7 ('Every font and asset in the shipped site has a recorded licence class' — called out as where 'legal exposure is concentrated') and G8 ('The tool is used more than twice' — called out as the goal most threatened by the product's own biggest risk) have no corresponding row in the §2.3 success-criteria table, unlike G1/G3/G5 which map cleanly to S1/S5, S3, S4.
why_it_matters: These are the two goals the PRD's own prose marks as highest-stakes (legal exposure, existential adoption risk), yet neither is operationalized into anything checkable. A goal with no measurement is a promise nobody has to keep.
suggested_fix: Add S8 ('zero shipped assets/fonts without a recorded licence class — grep against evidence bundle, build-failing') and S9 (a retention proxy, e.g. 'N sessions logged against the same ACOS project within 90 days') to §2.3, or explicitly state why they are intentionally unmeasured.

missing: Step 8's Inputs and Process both require 'the direction tour log' (recording the user's pick and stated reason across the direction tournament), but Step 4 — the only step that runs the tournament — lists its outputs as only `layout.json`, `content.json`, `provenance.json`. No step in §4 names or produces an artifact called a 'direction tour log.'
why_it_matters: Step 8's exit criterion requires 'evidence bundle is complete'; if the input artifact it depends on for that bundle section is never produced anywhere upstream, an implementer cannot build Step 8 as specified without guessing whether `provenance.json` is secretly this artifact under a different name.
suggested_fix: Either rename Step 4's `provenance.json` output to make clear it is the direction tour log, or add the direction tour log explicitly to Step 4's outputs list with its schema (direction ids shown, order, pick, stated reason).

missing: The tournament is specified as '3 at full size → pick → 3 → pick → head-to-head,' which as literally written shows the user at most two batches of 3 (6 directions) before a final head-to-head — with no stated round count or bracket structure explaining how all '~10 COMPLETE... design directions' that D1 requires be generated actually reach the user's view before one is chosen.
why_it_matters: D1 is a settled decision specifically about ~10 directions being generated; if the selection UI structurally only surfaces 6 of them, D1 is quietly weakened by the mechanism meant to implement it, and an engineer has no spec for what happens to the other ~4.
suggested_fix: State the full bracket explicitly (e.g., 'four rounds of 3, Swiss-style, covering all ~10 capsules; final two go head-to-head') or clarify that only a machine-prefiltered shortlist (not all ~10) enters the tournament, and name the prefilter.

missing: Neither the primary user (§3.1, the ACOS owner building the site) nor either named secondary user (§3.2, a future collaborator and the owner six months later) is the actual visitor of the published website. No stakeholder class in §3 represents the people who will use the finished site.
why_it_matters: The accessibility and legal obligations built into later sections (contrast gates, keyboard nav, licence attribution, WCAG-adjacent checks) exist to protect exactly this unnamed group. A 'Users and usage model' section that never identifies end visitors as a constrained stakeholder makes those downstream gates read as compliance boilerplate rather than something grounded in a named user this PRD says it serves.
suggested_fix: Add a third user class to §3, e.g. 'Tertiary: the published site's visitors — never interviewed, but every correctness gate (§13) exists to serve them,' and use it to justify why machine-enforced correctness (contrast, reflow, pause/stop) is non-negotiable even though the human is the aesthetic judge.

missing: §1's summary states LOCK unconditionally leads to publishing ('Then it publishes, with a licence-and-evidence bundle...'), but §4 Step 8 explicitly hedges: 'If deploy is not automated in v1, the PRD says so explicitly and emits a runbook.'
why_it_matters: A reader who only reads the framing summary (the document's stated purpose) comes away believing publish is guaranteed automatic; the pipeline detail two pages later says it may just be a manual runbook. That's a real capability overstatement in the section most likely to be quoted back as 'what was promised.'
suggested_fix: Soften §1 item 8 to 'Then it publishes — automatically if deploy is wired up, otherwise via a stated runbook' so the summary doesn't over-promise relative to Step 8's own hedge.

missing: The text claims 'Five hard-gated waves in fixed order' then enumerates six: (0) Continuity, (1) Strategy, (2) Taste, (3) Design-system specifics, (4) Constraints & admin, (5) Success criteria.
why_it_matters: A simple count error, but it leaves ambiguous whether wave 0 is really one of the 'five' gated waves or a separate zeroth phase that shouldn't be counted — which matters for how an implementer builds the wave-gating state machine (does the same hard-gate mechanism apply to Continuity, or is Continuity special-cased as already-resolved in Step 0?).
suggested_fix: Reword to 'Six phases (a completed continuity check plus five hard-gated waves)' or drop wave 0 from the enumerated list if it truly isn't gated within Step 1.

missing: '62 inventory items are app-shell/commerce/exotic-chart' is stated as a specific fact with no [V]/[I]/[A] source tag, unlike comparable claims elsewhere in these same sections (§1's Deque report and Anthropic-confirmed-April-2026 citations, §3.1's repo-context citation).
why_it_matters: The document's own sourcing convention (tag every non-obvious factual claim) is broken exactly where the claim is a specific number that gates an entire non-goal; without a tag there's no way to check whether 62 is a real count from the (unread-by-us) §7/§8 inventory or an estimate.
suggested_fix: Add a [V] or [I] tag pointing at the §7/§8 inventory count, or reword as an approximation ('roughly N items') if it hasn't been counted yet.

missing: Step 3 names its own mechanism the 'one-paste protocol' (one Cmd+A/Cmd+C per chunk), but S2's passing threshold is '≤3 pastes per chunk' — three times what the protocol's name promises — with no definition of what a 2nd or 3rd paste within one chunk represents (a retry after a failed parse? multiple content blocks?) or whether hitting 2-3 still counts as the protocol working.
why_it_matters: Testability: an implementer measuring S2 doesn't know whether 2 pastes in one chunk is a pass (within budget) or a signal the 'one-paste protocol' itself failed and should be logged as a defect.
suggested_fix: Either rename the mechanism ('bounded-paste protocol') to match its own stated tolerance, or clarify in §4 Step 3 that pastes beyond the first are retry-only and each retry should be logged as a near-miss against S2.

missing: Confirming: the recorded gaps-by-section.json entry for section '1' ('§§1-12.6 absent from reviewed text') was correctly identified as an artifact of the truncation bug per the task's explicit instruction, and was not re-reported here.
why_it_matters: N/A — this entry documents that the instruction to ignore that specific pre-recorded gap was followed, not a new defect.
suggested_fix: No action needed; informational only.

missing: A per-question skip map. §5 names four branch roots (has-existing-logo, needs-more-than-one-language, collects-personal-data, design-system-scoped-to-this-site-only) and claims each 'prunes ~10–12 questions', but nowhere lists which question IDs each branch suppresses, or on which answer value. Only four rows in the whole bank carry any dependency note (C2 'only if C1 ≠ fresh', L1 'no skips the rest of this section', X3 'only surfaced when wave-2 answers point dark', G1 'root of the legal-pages branch'), and those account for at most ~7 suppressible questions total, not 40–48.
why_it_matters: Branching is the sole mechanism that turns the 83-row bank into the '~35–45 answered' promise, and A19-A3 ('interview completes with ≤45 answered questions for a single-language, single-surface, no-forms marketing site') is a pass/fail acceptance criterion that cannot be evaluated without it. An engineer cannot build the question tree at all: 'has-existing-logo' maps to N7, but nothing states which of N8/N9/N10/N11/B1-B5/T6/D8 it does or does not suppress, and 'design-system-scoped-to-this-site-only' (D4) has no named dependents whatsoever. Arithmetic also fails: four gates at 10–12 each is 40–48 pruned questions, but the bank contains at most ~20 questions plausibly downstream of those four roots.
suggested_fix: Add a machine-readable dependency column to every row: `askIf` expression over prior question IDs and answer values (e.g. `askIf: N7 != 'none'`). Then assert the claim as a test: simulate the common-case answer set and assert the asked-count lands in 35–45, so A3 becomes checkable rather than asserted.

missing: A disambiguation between the tier namespace and the question-ID namespace. §5 defines tiers as `[T1]`/`[T2]`/`[T3]`, and Wave 2 then names ten questions T1–T10. Question T1 has tier T1; question T3 ('of the ones you hated…') has tier T1; question B4 has tier T3. §4 specifies the interview output as `00-interview/answers.json` (question-ID-keyed) and A4 requires that 'every emitted design directive in the Step-2 prompt cites the interview question ID that produced it.'
why_it_matters: The ID is the primary key of the whole pipeline: answers.json keys, the A4 provenance citations, the branch conditions, and any repair prompt naming a question. A directive citing 'T3' is irresolvably ambiguous between the negative-reference question and the inferred-with-default tier, and any grep, lint, or reviewer checking A4 will silently match the wrong thing. This is a rename that costs nothing now and is unfixable once answers.json files exist in prior projects that Step 0 warm-start reuses.
suggested_fix: Rename the tier labels (e.g. `[TIER-1]`/`[TIER-2]`/`[TIER-3]`, or `[must]`/`[jit]`/`[inferred]`) or renumber the Taste questions (e.g. TS1–TS10). State the ID grammar once as a rule: IDs are `<wave-prefix><n>`, prefixes are reserved, tier labels never collide.

missing: The prompt itself. §6 is titled 'the design-system generation prompt' but contains only a list of 16 things the prompt 'must demand' plus the return schema. There is no template, no worked prompt text, no statement of how `answers.json` fields map into prompt sections, no length target, and no specification of where the two artefacts the prompt depends on come from: the 'frozen token-name manifest' (demand 8) and the 'embedded, pinned OFL shortlist' with pre-subsetted base64 cuts (demands 4 and 5). §4 lists both as Step-2 *inputs* without defining them either.
why_it_matters: Step 2 of the user's eight-step vision is 'the skill GENERATES A PROMPT'. The generated prompt is the literal deliverable of this section, and A6 is an acceptance criterion asserting the prompt 'contains' seven named elements — untestable without a template defining what containment looks like. Demand 8's frozen manifest is the single mechanism that makes component swaps resolve (§6.1 states unnamed keys 'render unstyled with no error'), and its source is unspecified: is it §7's ~600–900 resolved token names, a subset, generated per direction, or hand-authored once? Demand 4's shortlist likewise has no size, no classification taxonomy, and no location, yet ingest hard-substitutes against it.
suggested_fix: Add §6.0: the prompt template with slot markers, the answers.json → slot mapping table (which gives A4 its provenance mechanically), and the file locations plus generation rules for `font-catalog.json` (with the pre-subsetted base64 strings §17-R2 says the skill supplies) and `token-manifest.json` (derived from §7, with an asserted key count).

missing: A single wire format. §6.2 specifies a manifest fenced block followed by 'every subsequent fenced block' opening with a `FILE:` comment, and the ingest contract 'splits on triple-backtick fences'. §6.4 specifies the opposite: 'one fenced block per chunk containing the manifest with inline file contents … One Cmd+A / Cmd+C per chunk.' The §6.2 examples are shown wrapped in four-backtick fences, but no escaping rule is ever stated for the nested-fence case §6.4 requires.
why_it_matters: These are two mutually exclusive parsers, and the section that defines the parser (§6.2, 'splits on triple-backtick fences') breaks under the format the section that defines the transport (§6.4) mandates — a single outer fence containing inner triple-backtick blocks either terminates early at the first inner fence or requires an unstated N-backtick convention the web model must be told to emit. §6.4 also claims the one-block format is what turns ~40 hand operations into ~5, and §17-R7 calls the paste marathon 'the most likely way the product quietly dies', so the transport format is load-bearing for the top adoption risk. A7 ('pasting a complete chunk ingests with zero manual file operations') cannot be implemented against two formats.
suggested_fix: Pick one and write it once. If §6.4 wins, state the fence-length rule explicitly (outer fence uses 5 backticks; no inner block may use ≥5), show a full nested worked example, and rewrite the ingest contract to parse the outer envelope first and inner blocks second. Add a round-trip test fixture: emit → paste → ingest → byte-compare.

missing: Per-item variant counts anywhere in the prompt demands or in the machine-checkable envelope. Demand 13 asks only for 'expected counts per group', and the manifest example shows `countsDeclared: {directions, components, artwork}`. §6.3's chunk B asks for 'identity-carrying component instances' with no number. §6 never references §7's or §8's variant-count tables, and never demands N variants per item.
why_it_matters: D1 settles '10 variants per swappable component on demand', §8.2 fixes the numbers by tier (A=10 or 12, B=3–6, C=20), and the user's one explicit completeness requirement is 'the components and suggested number of variants of each component'. As specified, a Stage-B response that returns one variant per component satisfies `countsDeclared.components == 22` and passes every ingest check in §6.2. The count discipline the PRD spends §8 establishing has no enforcement point at the boundary where the content actually arrives, and the failure is silent: the user reaches the component bar in Step 4 and finds nothing to swap to.
suggested_fix: Make `countsDeclared` per-item: `{"button-primary": 10, "marketing-hero": 12, …}` generated directly from §8.3's table by the prompt generator, and add an ingest row: 'per-item variant counts == declared, and declared == the §8 inventory for that item's tier → hard fail on the mismatching item with an auto-drafted repair prompt naming it.'

missing: A continuation or adaptive re-chunking protocol for a chunk that does not fit in one response. §6.2 detects truncation (terminator missing → hard fail) and A8 forbids writing a partial system. §6.3 pre-plans chunk boundaries by content, but §17-O2 states the real per-message output ceiling is unknown and unverifiable ('do not design around' the published figures). Nothing specifies what happens when a Stage-B chunk sized at ~40KB exceeds the ceiling.
why_it_matters: Under the specified behaviour the only recourse after a truncation is to re-paste the same chunk — which, if the chunk is simply larger than the ceiling, truncates again deterministically. The user loops. There is no 'continue from file 14', no rule for splitting a failing chunk in half and re-issuing, no instruction to the web model on how to resume (repeat the manifest? new terminator? re-emit already-received files?), and no ceiling-probe on first use to calibrate chunk size. Since the ceiling is explicitly unknown, the design must have a fallback and does not.
suggested_fix: Specify (a) a first-run calibration probe that measures the actual ceiling once and stores it in session.json; (b) a `continuation` field in the envelope (`{resumeAfter: "components/d03/button-primary/07.html"}`) with a matching skill-generated continuation prompt; (c) an automatic bisect rule: on a second truncation of the same chunk, split its file list in half and regenerate two prompts. Add an acceptance criterion covering the resume path, not just A8's clean rejection.

missing: Correct arithmetic. The bank contains 83 numbered rows, not 78. Counted: Wave 0 = 4; Wave 1 = 15 (P1–P5, B1–B5, A1–A5); Wave 2 = 10; Wave 3 = 13 (D1–D10, M1–M3); Wave 4 = 36 (N×11, X×6, L×4, G×3, H×6, U×2, Z×4); Wave 5 = 5. The running total reaches exactly 78 at the end of Wave 4 — Wave 5's five negative-constraint and success-criteria questions were never added.
why_it_matters: The wrong number is stated three times in §5, is repeated in §18 v1 scope-in ('Full interview (78 bank …)') and in §17-R21's own effort estimate ('the bank is 78 questions; at 30–60s each that is 40–80 minutes'), so the error propagates into the risk sizing and the delivery plan. More importantly, the five omitted questions are V1–V5 — the deny-list, the anti-reference, and the two LOCK-readiness questions — which are the highest-leverage rows in the bank per the PRD's own deny-list mechanism, and their omission from the count suggests Wave 5 was appended after the totals and branch-prune figures were computed.
suggested_fix: Correct to 83 in §5, §17-R21 and §18, and add a self-audit assertion (as §1's recorded gap suggests for §8): an asserted row count at the end of §5 that a script can verify against the table rows, so the number cannot drift again.

missing: Reconciliation with §17-R21, which states 'at 30–60s each that is 40–80 minutes before a single pixel', and an accounting for the non-question time. The 20–30 minute figure covers ~35–45 questions but also has to absorb T1 (sorting 24 images into love/neutral/hate), T2 and T3 (six written sentences of specific visual analysis), T4 (eight semantic-differential sliders), and B1 (a five-blank Geoffrey Moore positioning statement) — the four highest-effort tasks in the bank.
why_it_matters: Even at the pruned count and R21's own low-end 30s/question, 35–45 questions is 17–22 minutes with zero time for the swipe-sort or the written taste analysis; at R21's high end it is 45 minutes for the questions alone. §17-R21 names the interview as 'where the user's time is spent worst' and R7 identifies clerical burden as the way the product dies, so an advertised time that understates the real one by 2–3× is precisely the number most likely to produce abandonment at minute 25. The PRD contradicts itself on the single number the user sees before starting, and no acceptance criterion measures actual elapsed interview time.
suggested_fix: Either re-derive the advertised figure from R21's own per-question rate plus explicit budgets for the four heavy tasks (e.g. swipe-sort 4 min, taste sentences 3 min) and advertise that, or cut the bank until 20–30 minutes is true. Add an acceptance criterion: median wall-clock interview duration for the common case is within the advertised range, instrumented from day one.

section: 5 (Tier notation vs Delivery rules; tier distribution)
missing: Two unreconciled contradictions in the tier model. (1) Tier notation says `[T1]` 'gates the Step-2 prompt and must be answered'; the delivery rules say 'every taste question has an explicit "I don't know / surprise me" path'. The taste questions T1, T2, T3, T4, T6, T9, T10, D8, D9 and M1 are all tier-1 — they are simultaneously mandatory and skippable, and §4's Step-1 exit criterion ('all Tier-1 questions answered or explicitly defaulted') resolves it only by introducing a third state, 'explicitly defaulted', whose values are never listed. (2) Tier 3 is defined as 'inferred with a stated default and a visible change-this affordance' but is assigned to exactly one question in the entire bank (B4), and no default value is stated for it or for any other question except X2 (AA), M3 (yes), C4 (no), H1 (Cloudflare Pages), H3 (own repo) and Z4 (assume no).
why_it_matters: §5's own fallback flow says forced answers from a user with no real opinion 'misdirect the Step-2 prompt more than an honest non-answer', so the default value is the thing that actually reaches the prompt — and for ~77 of 83 questions it is unwritten. A reviewer cannot verify the recorded §5 gap's own suggested acceptance criterion ('records a stated default that appears in the concept document as skill-chosen') because there is nothing to compare against. A tier used once is also a signal the three-tier model was designed and then not applied.
suggested_fix: Add a `default` column to every row (value, or the rule that derives it from the swipe-sort results), state that a T1 question is satisfied by an answer OR a recorded default, and either populate tier 3 properly (most of the H/X/L/Z admin rows are natural T3 candidates) or drop the tier and say so.

missing: Four questions that downstream sections explicitly consume but that the bank never asks: (a) **site type** — §13.6 requires 'JSON-LD matched to the site-type answer (Organization/WebSite for marketing, VideoGame for game promo, WebApplication for app shell…)' and A70 gates on it; the closest question, P2, asks about business outcome (revenue/leads/hiring/portfolio/awareness), which does not map onto those schema.org types. (b) **primary/default language** — §13.6 requires `<html lang>` 'matching the interview language', but L1 only asks 'more than one language at launch? Which?' so a single-language project never records which language it is in. (c) **form submission destination** — §2-NG3 states 'forms use a third-party endpoint or a mailto fallback', and D7 asks which form *types* are needed, but nothing asks where submissions go; a contact form is therefore buildable and unshippable. (d) **claude.ai Projects / custom instructions** — §17-O27's stated resolution is literally 'Ask in the interview', and no such question exists (Z4 asks only about image-generation connectors).
why_it_matters: Each is a downstream gate or scope item resting on an interview answer that cannot exist. A70 is an acceptance criterion that no run can satisfy. §13.6's lang check will assert against an empty value on every single-language site — the common case the whole branching model is tuned for. The form-endpoint omission means the interview's own D7 branch produces a component with no destination, discovered at publish. O27 is recorded as resolved by a mechanism that was never built.
suggested_fix: Add four rows: site type as a closed list mapped 1:1 to the schema.org types §13.6 names (T1, Wave 1 near P2); primary content language (T1, promoted above L1 so it is asked unconditionally); form submission destination with the NG3 options named — third-party endpoint URL / mailto / none (T2, gated on D7 or any form component being selected); and claude.ai Projects availability (T2, beside Z4). Then add a cross-reference audit: every interview-derived value named in §13/§19 traces to a question ID.

missing: A question capturing which jurisdictions or markets the site serves. G1 asks whether personal data is collected, G2 asks which legal pages to produce, G3 asks about age-gates, region-blocks and regulated industries — none establishes where the business is established or where its visitors are, which is what determines whether GDPR/ePrivacy (consent banner required before non-essential cookies), the EU Accessibility Act, UK GDPR, CCPA/CPRA, or none of them apply.
why_it_matters: G2 offers to draft a privacy policy, terms and a cookie banner without ever asking which regime governs their contents, so the skill either drafts a generic document that satisfies no regulator or silently assumes one jurisdiction. The consent-banner question in particular is not a style choice: under ePrivacy a banner must block non-essential cookies before load, under CCPA it is an opt-out notice, and in neither-case it is unnecessary chrome. This also interacts with X1, which asks whether there is a legal accessibility requirement but leaves the user to know that the EAA applies to them — the interview should derive that, not test the user's legal knowledge.
suggested_fix: Add G0 (T1, root of the legal branch, asked before G1): 'Where is the business established, and which regions will visitors come from?' with a closed region list. Derive the applicable regimes from it, drive G2's document set and the consent-banner behaviour from that derivation, and use it to pre-answer X1 rather than asking the user to self-assess legal exposure.

section: 5 (Wave 4 — Z1) vs Branch roots / Ordering principle
missing: Correct placement of the time-budget question. Z1 ('How much of your time can you give — one sitting / a few short sessions / open-ended?') is noted as setting 'how aggressively to branch and how many variant rounds to offer', but it sits in Wave 4, after Waves 0–3 have already asked ~42 of the bank's 83 questions, including every taste and design-system question. Z2 ('a small number of strong options, or many to compare?') has the same problem: it is stated to 'directly set the D1 variant multiplier', which Stage A needs, yet it is asked near the end.
why_it_matters: A branching input that arrives after the questions it is supposed to prune has no effect on them — the aggressive-branch mode can only ever apply to the ~41 remaining admin questions, which are the cheap ones. The user who has 10 minutes is asked to spend 25 discovering that the skill would have shortened things had it known. §17-O18 separately asks whether the interview should split across sessions; that is a different question and does not cover this ordering defect.
suggested_fix: Move Z1 and Z2 into Wave 0 alongside the continuity check (they are cheap, non-taste, and set global policy), and state the concrete effect of each Z1 answer as a rule: which tiers are asked, which branches auto-default, and how many variant rounds are offered.

section: 5 (Brand assets — N7–N11; Content reality — N2; Wave 0 — C3)
missing: Any question about the licence or provenance of user-supplied visual assets. N9 asks about a web-embedding licence for a brand *typeface* only. C3 asks whether an artwork/sprite/photography library exists and where; N2 asks whether final photography/video exists; N10 asks about existing marketing materials. None asks who made them, under what licence, or whether redistribution on a public site is permitted.
why_it_matters: Step 8 of the user's vision is 'an evidence bundle listing every font and asset licence', and §13's gate 26 checks licence completeness. The only supply path for that data at intake is the interview, and it asks for licences on exactly one asset class. A user who points C3 at a folder of stock photos or client-supplied imagery produces a bundle where every non-font asset has an unknown licence, which either fails gate 26 at LOCK — after the site is built — or, worse, passes because the field was never populated. Font licensing is the well-handled case; the far more common raster-asset case is unhandled.
suggested_fix: Extend C3 and N2 with a licence sub-question per source (own work / commissioned with transferred rights / licensed stock — licence name and seat count / unknown), record it into `assets/manifest.json` at ingest, and make 'unknown' a blocking condition surfaced at intake rather than at LOCK.

missing: An integrity check on `sha256Prefix`. The envelope declares a `sha256Prefix` for every file and §4's Step-3 process states the skill 'validates against the envelope manifest (file list, line counts, sha256 prefixes, a per-run random terminator token)' — but §6.2's ingest table, which is the authoritative check list, contains no hash row. Line counts are the only per-file integrity check, and no normalisation rule is given (trailing newline, CRLF vs LF, whether the `FILE:` comment line counts, whether blank lines survive the paste).
why_it_matters: §17-R3 is titled 'Silent truncation produces valid, wrong CSS' and describes exactly the failure a hash catches and a line count does not: a direction's tokens cut after 40 of 62 properties inside a block that still parses. A block truncated at a line boundary passes a line-count check trivially; a block whose whitespace was normalised by the clipboard fails one spuriously. §4 claims the strong check runs and §6.2 does not implement it, so which behaviour ships depends on which section the implementer reads.
suggested_fix: Add a hash row to §6.2's table above the line-count row ('sha256 of the file body, first 6 hex chars, matches declared → hard fail on that file'), specify the exact bytes hashed (body after the FILE: line, LF-normalised, single trailing newline), and either delete the line-count check as redundant or state it as the cheap pre-filter.

missing: Reconciliation between smallest-first ordering and the no-partial-write rule. §6.2 orders files smallest-first 'so a truncation loses the least', but A8 states that pasting a truncated chunk 'fails with a message naming the missing files, and does not write a partial system'. §6.2's own table also has the terminator check as a hard fail while the countsDeclared check ingests everything present — two different truncation responses in one table.
why_it_matters: If a truncated chunk writes nothing, the ordering saves nothing and the stated rationale is false. If partial ingest does occur (as the countsDeclared row implies), smallest-first is actively the wrong order: it guarantees the last thing emitted is the largest file, which for a Stage-B chunk is `tokens/dNN.tokens.json` (412 lines in §6.2's own example) — the one file without which every component in the chunk renders unstyled and the direction cannot be previewed at all. 'Loses the least' is optimising file count while sacrificing the only file with fan-out. An implementer cannot pick a behaviour, and §17-R3's mitigation list cites smallest-first ordering as one of five defences against the corruption-without-symptom class.
suggested_fix: State one truncation policy (recommended: write nothing on a missing terminator, so A8 holds), then re-order by dependency rather than size — tokens first, then components, then artwork — and delete the smallest-first rationale, since under a no-partial-write policy the emission order is irrelevant to loss and relevant only to how much of a repaste is reusable.

missing: An arithmetic reconciliation. Chunk A is specified as '~10 direction capsules (26-slot vector + 40–80 word manifesto each) + ONE gallery artifact previewing all 10' and sized as 'Small; fits reliably'. Demand 5 requires 'a base64 data:font/woff2 @font-face for each direction's display face', which §6.1 itself sizes at ~11–27KB base64 per face. Ten directions previewed in one gallery artifact therefore carry 110–270KB of base64 font data — roughly 30–70K tokens — inside the chunk called small.
why_it_matters: Chunk A is the chunk the design depends on fitting: §6.3 states it 'is what the user actually judges' and the whole thin-Stage-A rationale rests on it being cheap. If it does not fit, the user's first contact with the product is a truncation. The section supplies both numbers and never multiplies them. §17-O2 additionally says the real ceiling is unmeasured, so there is no headroom argument available either.
suggested_fix: Do the arithmetic explicitly in §6.3 with a stated token budget for chunk A. If it does not fit, resolve it: subset the gallery fonts to the ~40 glyphs actually rendered in a hero card rather than the full preview glyph set, or have the skill inject the base64 locally into a gallery it assembles itself (it already owns the pinned font catalog per demand 4) so the web model never transports font bytes at all.

missing: Any specification of what an artwork is on the wire. The chunking table's third row reads 'Art | The 20 artworks with suitsDirections[] tags | Variable' and that is the entire treatment. No format (inline SVG? data-URI raster? a code-drawn canvas/CSS fragment?), no per-artwork size budget, no file-naming convention in the manifest, no `FILE:` example, and no reconciliation with §17-R1's finding that claude.ai has no raster generation and that '20 flat geometric SVGs come back — the exact AI-slop register the anti-slop lint detects'.
why_it_matters: Artwork/background style is one of the two categories the user named by example (FruitSync), D1 fixes the count at 20, and §17-O15 is still open on whether '20 artworks' means 20 pieces or 20 style sets. §6 is the section that has to turn that into a wire format and it declines to. 'Variable' is not a budget, so the chunking strategy — whose entire purpose is fitting output inside an unknown ceiling — has no number for the one payload most likely to be large. An implementer building the ingest has no artwork branch to write.
suggested_fix: Specify the artwork wire format explicitly per lane (§17's Lane A code-drawn: an SVG or CSS/canvas fragment with a `FILE: artwork/aNN.svg` header, token-referencing per A20, hard size cap stated; Lane B: a manifest reference into the detected asset library, no bytes transported; Lane C: explicitly out of the paste channel with its own runbook). Give the Art chunk a token budget and a per-artwork byte cap, and state which lane §6.3's Art chunk actually covers.

missing: A statement of which parts of §6 apply to the local path. §6.5 says only 'the same prompt, the same schema, run against a Claude Code subagent', and A12 asserts the local bundle 'passes the identical validator'. But §6.1's demands 5, 6, 7 and 15 exist solely because of the claude.ai artifact CSP and preview surface; §6.3's entire chunking strategy exists because of the 200K shared context and the one-artifact-per-turn rule; and §6.2's envelope (per-run terminator as 'the very last line of the response', one-paste ordering) describes a chat response that does not exist when a subagent writes files directly.
why_it_matters: Local Regeneration Mode is v1 scope-in (§18) and the PRD's strongest lever against its top risk, so it is not a footnote path. As written, the 'identical validator' either rejects a locally-written bundle for having no terminator line, or the terminator check is silently skipped locally — in which case the truncation defence §17-R3 depends on does not exist on the path the PRD expects to be used most. The demands that constrain design quality (vanilla-only, base64 fonts, 390px preview) are also either pointlessly binding locally or quietly dropped, and either way the two paths no longer produce comparable output for the same prompt.
suggested_fix: Add a column to §6.1's table marking each demand web-only / both / local-only, and a short §6.5 subsection stating the local envelope contract: what replaces the terminator (per-file write completion plus hash verification at write time), whether chunking applies at all locally, and which checks in §6.2's table are no-ops. Reword A12 to assert equivalence of the *validated properties*, not of the validator.

missing: A conversation-management rule. Demand 8 requires the frozen token-name manifest 're-pasted verbatim in every chunk' and demand 9 requires all prior-direction parameters as negative constraints 'in every subsequent chunk' — both of which are only necessary if chunks may span separate conversations. §6.3 computes total volume against 'a 200K claude.ai context that artifacts count against' but never states how many chunks fit in one conversation, when the user should start a new one, or what the skill tells them to do at that boundary.
why_it_matters: Stage A (~10 capsules plus a gallery artifact) followed by three Stage-B expansions at ~40KB each, with the frozen manifest and accumulating negative constraints re-pasted every time, plausibly exhausts a single conversation partway through the run — and the failure mode is not an error, it is degraded output or a refusal mid-chunk. The user is the one operating the browser and has been given no instruction. §17-O2 flags the ceiling as unknown ('the difference between 2 conversations and 12') but §6 does not carry a design that works under either answer.
suggested_fix: State a conversation policy: one conversation per chunk by default (which makes demands 8 and 9 necessary rather than incidental and removes the context-exhaustion variable entirely), with the skill emitting each chunk's prompt as a self-contained paste and telling the user in plain words to start a fresh chat for each. If §17-O27 resolves that Projects are available, note the variant where the schema lives in project instructions.

section: 6.2 (ingest contract — contrast row and JSON row)
missing: Two numeric/behavioural specifications. The contrast row says 'auto-nudge OKLCH lightness deterministically; if the fix exceeds a delta threshold, flag for human confirm' with no threshold value and no statement of the nudge step size or search direction. The JSON row says 'attempt a tolerant repair pass (trailing commas, obvious syntax slips)' with no bounded list of what counts as an obvious slip.
why_it_matters: Neither is implementable or testable as written. The contrast nudge silently alters the user's chosen colours — the exact values that carry the direction's identity — so the threshold is the line between an invisible correction and a visible change to a design the user picked; A10 tests that a failing pair is 'detected, auto-nudged, and logged' without any bound on how far. 'Obvious syntax slips' is an open-ended licence for a repair pass to rewrite untrusted pasted content, which is the same channel §12.14 treats as a security boundary.
suggested_fix: State the nudge algorithm and bound (e.g. adjust OKLCH L in 0.01 steps toward the nearest passing value, maximum ΔL 0.05, else flag) and enumerate the exact repair transforms permitted (trailing comma removal, single→double quotes, unquoted key quoting — nothing else), with everything auto-fixed written to `import-report.json`.

missing: A reconciliation between §10's per-feature priority column and §18's phase plan. They assign different phases to at least fifteen features. §10.1 marks real-grid overlay, snap engine, smart alignment guides, align tools, padding/gap drag handles, drag-to-place, span resize, breakpoint switcher, per-breakpoint override and keyboard nudge as **v1**; §18's 'Scope cut (explicit)' removes all of them from v1 ('No canvas drag. No gridlines, no snapping, no free-position, no zoom/pan'; 'No per-breakpoint override authoring') and lists them in v2's 'real-grid canvas' bullet. §10.2 marks multi-select and breadcrumb v1; §18 cuts multi-select from v1 and lists breadcrumb in v2. §10.6 marks live contrast checker, scoped axe-core and the motion checks v1; §18 lists 'Live a11y/contrast lint inline, motion-property lint, text-spacing stress clone, off-token advisory' in v2. §10.7 marks per-section notes→regeneration and the comment schema v1; §18 lists them in v2.
why_it_matters: Priority is the only thing §10 adds beyond a feature list, and it is wrong for roughly a seventh of the surface. An engineer building from §10 ships the canvas in v1; an engineer building from §18 ships none of it. The two sections are each written as normative. This also silently determines whether D2 (constraint dragging) exists at all in the first shipping version — the exact deviation the recorded §18 gap says needs user sign-off, except here it is not even self-consistent enough to sign off on.
suggested_fix: Make §18 the single source of phase truth and regenerate §10's priority column from it mechanically, or delete the priority column from §10 and reference §18. Then add an assertion to the PRD's own self-audit that every §10 row appears in exactly one §18 phase list.

missing: A definition of the swappable unit for motion. §9.2 gives each container kind a count of 'structural variants' (e.g. CSS/GSAP DOM container = 8); §9.3 gives each animation kind a separate count (e.g. hero entrance = 8, hover micro-reactions = 10); §12.3 stores motion as neither — as `props.motion: "entrance.mask-wipe@03"`, a preset id on an `ArtContainer` node, while `variant: "background-scene@07"` is a different field. Nothing states what the component bar shows when an animated container is selected: 8 container variants, 8 hero-entrance variants, both in one list, or a separate motion picker. Nor is it stated whether the two counts multiply (a container × kind matrix) or are alternatives.
why_it_matters: D4 settles that motion is an ordinary design-system item with variants, and Step 4(d) is 'a component bar to swap any component for a comparable variant.' If the swap unit for motion is undefined, D4 is honoured in prose and unbuilt in the data model — the one field the editor actually mutates (`props.motion`) is not a `variant` at all, so the component bar has no defined behaviour for the single container family the user named twice (background art, animation for the front). It also makes the variant counts in §9.2/§9.3 uncheckable against the user's completeness requirement, because nobody can say which of the two numbers is the '10 variants on demand' number D1 settles.
suggested_fix: State one model: e.g. the container kind is the component, its structural variants are what the bar swaps, and the animation kind + variant is a `props.motion` token reference with its own picker showing §9.3's counts. Then show the resulting node in §12.3 with both fields populated, and state explicitly whether §9.2 and §9.3 counts multiply.

missing: Any cell-occupancy or collision policy. §11.2 gives one formula that computes a start column only — it never derives `row`, never says what happens to the block's existing span, never covers a drop that crosses a section boundary, and never states what the editor does when the target cells are already occupied by a sibling (swap the two blocks, push siblings down, allow the overlap, or reject the drop). §11.8 failure #1 detects overlap after the fact per breakpoint, which is a detector, not a drop-time rule. §10.1 says commit writes `{col, colSpan, row, rowSpan}` but no text derives row or rowSpan from a pointer position.
why_it_matters: This is the product's headline mechanic (Step 4b, 'drag-movable components') and the section that exists to specify it. Occupancy policy is the hardest and most consequential decision in a grid editor — it determines whether dragging one block silently displaces three others, and whether a user can create the overlapping mess §11.3 spends a table proving Squarespace shipped. An engineer cannot write the drop handler from what is here, and no test can be written for behaviour that is not stated.
suggested_fix: Specify the full drop algorithm: row derivation from pointer Y against resolved track positions, span preservation on move vs clamp at the grid edge, the occupied-cell rule (recommend: allow same-cell stacking only for explicitly z-ordered art containers, otherwise displace-down within the section with a live ghost showing the displacement), the cross-section drop rule, and a rejected-drop visual. Add one acceptance criterion per branch.

missing: A reconciliation of the free-position implementation with the platform constraint stated two subsections later. §11.4 rule 1 requires the free element to keep 'a declared anchor (parent edge, **sibling**, or grid cell)' with a percentage/`clamp()` offset from it, and §12.3 encodes exactly that as `anchor: {to: "parent"|nodeId, edge: ...}`. §11.5 then rules that 'Anchor positioning is still a carryover Interop 2026 item — use it only for editor chrome and progressive-enhancement decoration, **never load-bearing layout**.' CSS has no other way to offset one element from an arbitrary non-parent sibling without either anchor positioning or runtime JS measurement — and runtime JS is forbidden in the locked output by §12.5's no-editor-runtime contract.
why_it_matters: The escape hatch D2 grants the user is specified in a form that the PRD's own platform section forbids, and the persisted schema in §12.3 has already committed to it. Either sibling anchors are unbuildable in the exported site (so the hatch is parent-and-grid-cell only, which must be said, because it changes what the user can express), or the locked site ships positioning JS, which breaks D3. Both consequences are large and neither is acknowledged.
suggested_fix: Restrict `anchor.to` to `parent` or a grid cell/line for v1, delete `nodeId` from §12.3's schema, and state the restriction as a named limitation of the escape hatch. If sibling anchoring is genuinely required, specify the compile strategy (e.g. promote the pair into a shared subgrid wrapper at generate time) and prove it needs no runtime code.

missing: Consistency in cascade direction. §11.3's verdict is normative: 'desktop-down cascade with sparse per-breakpoint overrides', base = desktop, overrides attach to *smaller* breakpoints, and 'blocks with no small-breakpoint override compile to `grid-column: 1 / -1`'. §12.3's canonical node — the one an implementer will copy — encodes the opposite: `default` spans 12 columns and an **`lg`** key narrows it to span 10, i.e. a mobile-first base with a larger-breakpoint override. The breakpoint key names (`lg`) also do not match the switcher labels in §10.1 (390 / 768 / 1280 / full) or the sets used by the gates.
why_it_matters: §12.3 is the save format. If the persisted keys mean 'override upward' while the layout rules mean 'override downward', every page inverts: sparse overrides land on the wrong side of the cascade and the `1 / -1` mobile default in §11.3 can never fire, which is the single rule §11.3 credits with preventing the documented Squarespace overlap epidemic. A reader cannot tell which of two normative statements to implement.
suggested_fix: Rewrite the §12.3 example desktop-down: `default` = the 1280 layout, with `md`/`sm` (or `768`/`390`) keys carrying narrowing overrides, and state the exact key vocabulary once, shared by §10.1's switcher, §11.3's cascade, §11.4's lock gate and §12.3's schema.

missing: Fields the contract needs to be instantiable and enforceable: (a) no asset/source reference at all (no `src`, sequence path, Lottie/Rive file, or video URL) even though §9.5 governs formats and `assets/manifest.json` is the allowlist every reference is validated against; (b) no loop/iteration policy, autoplay flag or muted flag, though §9.2's video row says 'muted is browser law'; (c) no video poster frame (the only poster field is `reducedMotionPoster`, which is a different thing); (d) no performance cost class, though §9.5 caps containers per page by cost and the recorded §13 gap asks for a lock gate 'keyed to container cost class'; (e) no reference to the reduced-motion **variant**, only a poster, though §10.6's v1 check is 'confirm the placed item's catalog includes a tagged reduced variant'; (f) no enumeration of the legal values of `trigger` or the units/range of `viewportThreshold` — the only value given anywhere is '~20%' in prose.
why_it_matters: The contract is presented as the one thing every art and motion container implements, and §9.1 rule 3 makes `trigger` + `viewportThreshold` the fields that decide which animation a container performs — so an unenumerated `trigger` makes the central mechanism of D4 unimplementable. Without a source field the generator has nothing to validate against the asset manifest; without a cost class the concurrency caps in §9.5 cannot be computed; without a reduced-motion variant ref the v1 check in §10.6 has nothing to read.
suggested_fix: Extend the contract block with `source {kind, ref, poster}`, `playback {autoplay, muted, loop, iterationCount}`, `costClass: 'free'|'cheap'|'heavy'|'gpu'`, `reducedMotionVariantRef`, and an explicit closed enum for `trigger` (page-load, viewport-enter, viewport-scrub, pointerenter, click, always) with `viewportThreshold` typed as a 0–1 fraction, defaulted per trigger.

missing: Agreement between the subsection heading and the table: the heading says '11 structural types' and the table lists 16 rows (still-image, CSS/GSAP DOM, decorative background, marquee, reveal-on-enter, cursor-effect layer, sprite, video-loop, vector, pinned/scrubbed, SVG mask, canvas/WebGL, particle, kinetic type, cursor-reactive, sticky/pin). No note explains which five are excluded from the count or why.
why_it_matters: The user's explicit completeness requirement is that the PRD carries the components and a suggested variant count for each. A stated total that disagrees with its own table by five items makes the inventory uncountable — a reviewer cannot certify completeness, and the recorded fix for the whole-document gap (a self-audit table with an asserted row count) will fail on this section first. It also propagates: §8 line 319's v1 list names motion items ('reveal container', 'section reveal', 'text reveal', 'hover set', 'easing matrix') that do not map one-to-one onto either §9.2's or §9.3's rows.
suggested_fix: Correct the heading to 16 (or split the table into a v1 core and a gated extension set with two stated counts), and add a mapping row-by-row from §8's v1 motion list to §9.2/§9.3 ids so the two inventories are provably the same set.

section: 9.5 (asset-supply gap) — unresolved by the PRD's own instruction
missing: The decision the row demands. It states that video-loop and image-sequence containers 'cannot be populated by the claude.ai leg' and that 'the PRD must state which' of three outcomes applies (user supplies footage, external provider with a licence manifest, or out of scope for v1) — then never states it, deferring to §17-R1. Meanwhile both containers remain in §9.2 with priorities (v2) and variant counts (3 each) as though deliverable.
why_it_matters: This is a silent scope cut of two catalogued container kinds, recorded as an instruction to a future editor rather than as a decision requiring user sign-off. A builder reading §9.2 will scope three video-loop variants; a builder reading §9.5 will scope none. Because the external-provider branch drags in a third-party licence chain, it also changes the Step-8 evidence bundle. The recorded §18 gap covers artwork lanes (A/B/C) but not video or frame sequences, so this is unhandled anywhere.
suggested_fix: Pick one now and write it into §9.2's rows: recommend video-loop and sprite/frame-sequence marked 'user-supplied asset required — container ships, generator never fabricates the asset', with an interview question capturing whether the user has footage, and an explicit out-of-scope note if they do not.

missing: A phase home for §9.6's three mitigations. PREVIEW MOTION, the per-container scrub slider and the trigger-point markers are presented as the answer to the section's own stated contradiction, but §10.8 prices 'Motion preview toggle' at v2 and §18 puts 'Motion preview toggle, per-container scrub, trigger markers' in v2. Yet §9.2/§9.3 place marquee, reveal-on-enter, hero entrance, hover micro-reactions, custom cursor, background ambient motion and smooth scroll in v1. It is also never stated whether §10.8's v1 'In-editor Preview mode' plays motion or freezes it like edit mode.
why_it_matters: As phased, v1 ships eight motion kinds that the user can select but cannot see move anywhere in the tool — the §9.6 failure loop ('they cannot debug the thing they are trying to fix') is not partially mitigated in v1, it is fully unmitigated, and §9.6 claims otherwise. §10.8's v1 'Reduced-motion preview' compounds this: the user can preview the reduced variant but not the full one it is reduced from.
suggested_fix: Move PREVIEW MOTION (the cheapest of the three — it is 'stop editing, unfreeze tweens') into v1 in both §10.8 and §18, keep scrub and trigger markers at v2, and state explicitly in §10.8 whether In-editor Preview mode plays motion.

missing: The mechanism behind 'Re-anchoring triggers a scroll-length resimulation before the preview is shown accurate.' Nothing defines what is simulated, what quantity is computed, what threshold counts as insufficient scroll room, or what the editor does when the target section fails that threshold — reject the drop, auto-extend the section's min-block-size, shorten the timeline, or warn and proceed. There is also no lock-time gate asserting that every pinned sequence still has room at 390/768/1280, even though §11.4's free-position gate is specified at exactly that level of detail.
why_it_matters: §9.4 identifies this as 'the one drag-fragile container' and then hand-waves its only mitigation. Pin-without-room is a silent failure — the composition does not error, it just plays wrong — so an unspecified detector means the failure ships. It is also the one place where a container's validity depends on its neighbours' heights, which is precisely the case a per-node validator will miss.
suggested_fix: Define the resimulation as: after re-anchor, compute the parent's scrollable height at each breakpoint, require `pinDuration <= availableScroll * k` (state k), and on failure block the drop with a named reason plus a one-click 'extend section to fit'. Add a lock gate asserting the inequality holds at every breakpoint.

missing: The touch counterpart the section requires but never specifies. §9.3 states hover micro-reactions 'must have a touch equivalent — a hover-only affordance is a usability defect', but no equivalent is defined for any of the ten variants, and no gate verifies one exists. §9.2's global cursor-effect layer (5 variants) 'must disable on coarse pointers' and all five cursor-reactive variants 'no-op on touch', so the custom-cursor item — Tier A, 10 variants in §9.3, named explicitly by the user — has no defined appearance on the majority of visits, and §7's `direction.signature-moment` may sit on top of it.
why_it_matters: A user-named design-system item that is structurally invisible to mobile visitors is a coverage hole the user should be told about, and 'must have a touch equivalent' as written is a vibe, not a requirement: nothing enumerates the equivalents and nothing checks them. It also touches WCAG — information or affordances conveyed only on hover cannot be reached by a touch or keyboard user, and §13's gate list has no hover-parity check.
suggested_fix: Add a `touchEquivalent` field to each hover/cursor variant naming its :active or focus-visible counterpart, state what the direction renders on coarse pointers in place of the custom cursor (recommend: the cursor item is desktop-only decoration and the direction must carry a non-cursor signature for touch), and add a lint asserting every interactive element with a hover treatment also has a focus-visible and :active treatment.

missing: Consistency on what the browser sends the server. §10.4 specifies autosave as 'A small JSON diff POSTed to the server and written to disk.' §12.13 rule 1 forbids exactly that: 'The client never sends a file path or a file body. It sends a typed semantic op … and the server derives the JSON Patch. Raw-JSON-Patch-over-HTTP is nearly as dangerous as raw paths.'
why_it_matters: §12.13 is a security control with a stated threat (an op that rewrites `systemLock` or injects an `override` path), and §10.4 describes the wire format that defeats it. Whichever an implementer reads first becomes the protocol. It also affects the op log: §12.9 layer (a) derives `patch`/`inverse` server-side from typed ops, which cannot happen if the client already sent the diff.
suggested_fix: Rewrite §10.4's autosave row as 'debounced flush of the pending typed-op queue to POST /ops; the server derives and applies the JSON Patch and appends to history.jsonl', and cross-reference §12.13.

missing: One name for the source of truth. §12.2's file set has no `layout.json` — the scene graph is `pages/<id>.doc.json`, one per page. But §10.2 stores clipboard fragments as `layout.json` fragments, §10.4 puts the undo stack 'over `layout.json`', §11.8 rows 4 and 11 say the same, §12.6 persists the op log 'alongside `layout.json`', §12.10 has Claude and the browser both writing `layout.json`, and §4 and §18 list `layout.json` as a v1 deliverable. §12.13's write allowlist then permits only `pages/*.doc.json`.
why_it_matters: It is not cosmetic: a single `layout.json` implies one site-wide undo stack and one lock file; per-page `doc.json` implies per-page stacks, per-page optimistic-concurrency tokens, and a defined behaviour for undoing an edit made on a page you have since navigated away from — a v1 feature, since multi-page is v1 scope. As written the write allowlist in §12.13 does not permit writes to the file §12.10's conflict story is entirely about, so the conflict mitigation has no legal write path.
suggested_fix: Rename every occurrence to `pages/<id>.doc.json`, and state explicitly whether the command stack, the op log and the editor lock are per-page or site-wide (recommend site-wide stack keyed by page id, so cross-page undo is defined).

missing: Write paths for four doc-owned files. §12.13 permits the server exactly three path shapes — `pages/*.doc.json`, `history.jsonl`, `.wb/**` — but §12.7's zone table assigns `content.json` and `site.json` to 'the editor process only', §12.1 names `content.json` part of the composition tier the editor mutates, and §12.2 makes `assets/manifest.json` and `provenance.json` editor-maintained records. Several v1 features write to those files: per-page SEO/meta fields and the multi-page manager (page list lives in `site.json`), the asset/media manager and image auto-optimisation on drop (`assets/manifest.json`), and inline text editing if copy lives in `content.json`.
why_it_matters: Four v1 editor features have no legal write path under the security rule, and A78 in §19 asserts the three-path rule as a test — so the acceptance suite will fail the product's own v1 scope, or the rule will be quietly widened at implementation time, which is how path allowlists stop being allowlists.
suggested_fix: Extend the allowlist to the exact doc-owned set (`pages/*.doc.json`, `content.json`, `site.json`, `assets/manifest.json`, `provenance.json`, `history.jsonl`, `.wb/**`), keep the `realpath` + prefix + no-symlink assertions, and update A78. State which typed ops may touch `site.json` and forbid ops from writing `systemLock` at all.

missing: How the second build is produced. The gate requires building the same doc twice, 'once with the editor integration installed, once with it removed from `package.json` entirely', and requires byte-identical trees. Nothing specifies how that removal happens inside `wb lock` — whether the lock command mutates `package.json` and the lockfile and reinstalls, or builds from a pristine copied tree, what happens to a running design server sharing `node_modules`, or how long it takes. Nor does anything establish that the Astro/Vite build itself is byte-reproducible: §12.8 constrains the *generator*'s determinism only, and the recorded §12.8 gap already notes binary assets are unaudited.
why_it_matters: This gate is the PRD's stated proof of D3 — 'this converts "the editor doesn't ship" from an intention into a CI fact' — and §18 makes 'a passing two-build byte-equality check' the v1 exit criterion. A gate with no mechanism cannot be built, and a byte-equality assertion over a build system whose reproducibility is unestablished will either fail spuriously (and be disabled) or pass vacuously.
suggested_fix: Specify the mechanism: `git worktree` or rsync to a clean temp tree, `npm ci` against a variant lockfile with the integration dependency omitted, build with `--outDir`, compare with a manifest of SHA-256 per file. Add the reproducibility preconditions explicitly (no build timestamps, deterministic chunk hashing, `SOURCE_DATE_EPOCH` pinned) and a wall-clock budget.

missing: A handling path for hand-edits made to the exported tree. Row 6 promises unlock 'diffs the exported tree and shows hand-edits instead of discarding them' — but showing is not preserving. `dist/published/` is regenerated wholesale on the next LOCK, §12.5 says the restore path is 'documents only, never `dist/`', and `wb extract-override` in §12.7 lifts fragments from `src/generated/**`, not from `dist/`. So the diff is displayed once and the edit is then lost on the next lock, with no route back into the doc.
why_it_matters: The task of §12.6 is to make LOCK/UNLOCK losses either impossible or explicitly named. This row names a loss and then claims a handling that does not preserve anything. Because §12.5's headline claim is 'there is no unlock transformation to get wrong', a reader will trust it and lose work — the same silent-loss class §12.10 devotes a whole subsection to preventing.
suggested_fix: Either state plainly that edits to `dist/published/` are unrecoverable by design and make the diff a blocking prompt at the next LOCK ('N hand-edits in the published tree will be overwritten — review / discard'), or extend `wb extract-override` to accept a dist-side fragment and re-home it into `src/overrides/`. Name whichever is chosen in the ledger row.

missing: A rule for what `render(doc, systemLock, library)` does when a node's `component` or `variant` id is not present in the library. This happens on at least three normal paths: Step 5 regenerating a new design system or a new direction (every node's variant ref is from the old direction), restoring an older lock via `git checkout wb-lock/<n> -- pages/ site.json` against a library that has since changed, and cross-direction swaps (v2 in §18). `system.lock.json` pins the imported system so it cannot change *silently*, but nothing says what happens when it changes deliberately.
why_it_matters: The render function is declared pure and the doc is declared the only truth, so an unresolvable reference has to resolve to something: a hard error that blocks the editor from opening, a placeholder that ships as a hole, or a mapped fallback. Step 5 ('if nothing looks good, generate a brand-new design-system prompt') is a user-named step in the authoritative vision, and it is the exact operation that invalidates every variant reference on every page. No migration policy, no gate, and no acceptance criterion covers it.
suggested_fix: Define a resolution policy in §12.1: unknown component id = hard fail with a named report; unknown variant id within a known component = fall back to the direction's canonical variant with a per-node 'variant migrated' flag surfaced in the editor and blocking LOCK until acknowledged. Add a `wb migrate` op that rewrites variant refs when the system lock changes, and a gate asserting zero unresolved refs before LOCK.

missing: What 'auto-demotes to normal flow at ≤479px' actually produces. A free-positioned element has no flow position — that is what free-position means — so nothing defines where it lands: its order among siblings, its column/span at the small breakpoint, its z-order relative to blocks it used to float over, or whether the demotion is authored into the doc (visible and overridable) or applied at render time (invisible). §12.3's `mode: "free"` object carries `anchor`, `offset` and `z` and no flow fallback. Separately, 479px is not a breakpoint the editor can display: §10.1's switcher offers 390/768/1280/full, §11.4's own lock gate renders 390/768/1440, and §11.7 pins four device sizes none of which is 479.
why_it_matters: The escape hatch's small-screen behaviour is the whole reason D2 grants it conditionally, and it is the one behaviour a user cannot predict or inspect. As written the user drags an element free at 1280, and at 390 it reappears somewhere the tool never showed them, in an order nobody chose. Because the demotion boundary is outside every previewable and gated width, the transition itself is untestable.
suggested_fix: Store an explicit `flowFallback: {col, span, order}` on every free-positioned node, defaulted at drop time from the element's visual position and editable; state that demotion is authored into the doc, not implicit at render; and either move the demotion boundary to 390 (a previewable breakpoint) or add 479 to the switcher and to §11.4's lock-gate render set.

missing: A per-breakpoint order control and a rule reconciling DOM order with desktop visual order. §11.3 says blocks with no small override compile to `grid-column: 1 / -1` 'in source order', but explicit `grid-column`/`grid-row` integers (§11.1 level 3, §11.6's promotion rule) let the desktop visual order diverge arbitrarily from DOM order. DOM order simultaneously drives the mobile stack, the tab order and the screen-reader order. §10.1's anchor verbs offer 'order (up/down among siblings)' with no per-breakpoint scope, so changing the mobile stack necessarily changes desktop auto-placement, tab order and screen-reader order too.
why_it_matters: Mobile stacking order is the second half of the failure class §11.3 spends a whole comparison table on — Squarespace blocks 'mix-up or change order and position' is quoted in that very table — and only the overlap half is addressed. It is also a live WCAG exposure: SC 1.3.2 Meaningful Sequence (Level A) and SC 2.4.3 Focus Order (Level A) are broken by exactly this divergence, and §10.6/§13 offer only a post-hoc heuristic flag with no mechanism to fix a flagged case, because no order control exists that does not break something else.
suggested_fix: State the invariant that DOM order is always the intended reading order and desktop visual order must be achieved by grid placement, never by reordering DOM; add a per-breakpoint `order` override in the layout node with a warning that it desynchronises visual from reading order (and a lint that blocks it where the element is focusable); and add a small-breakpoint stack-order preview showing the resulting sequence before commit.

missing: An accurate count. The preamble states '~35 of ~95 items are v1.' The section's tables contain 113 priced rows: 71 v1, 37 v2, 5 v3 (counted mechanically). The v1 figure is off by roughly 2x and the total by ~19%.
why_it_matters: This number is the section's only summary of scope and it is the input to the v1 effort estimate and the phased plan. A 71-item v1 editor is a materially different product from a 35-item one, and the Canva comparison in the same paragraph (which argues for restraint) is doing rhetorical work that the actual table does not support. It also compounds the §10-vs-§18 phase contradiction: the true v1 count under §18's cuts is different again, and neither number is stated.
suggested_fix: Recount mechanically and state three numbers: total rows, v1 under §10's column, and v1 under §18's phase plan (they should be equal once the phase contradiction is fixed). Assert the counts in the PRD self-audit so they cannot drift again.

missing: An authoring surface for chart data in the version that ships charts. §10.3 prices 'Table/data editor for charts' at **v3** and 'Custom-component insertion' at **v2**, while §18's v1 scope cut says 'Charts: build-time SVG only, ≤4 mark types' — i.e. charts exist in v1 — and §14.6 specifies four chart parts and 'required' data states. Nothing states how a v1 chart receives its data, or how the user places one at all given custom-component insertion is v2.
why_it_matters: Charts and graphs are the example the user gave for Step 6 ('the user may add custom components not normally included — for example graphs or charts'), so this is a user-named capability. As phased, v1 renders charts nobody can populate, and the surface for populating them arrives two versions later. Either charts are not really in v1 or the data editor is not really v3, and neither reading is written down.
suggested_fix: Decide and align all three sections: recommend a minimal v1 CSV/table paste field bound to the chart node's props (cheap, no spreadsheet), keep the full spreadsheet-grade editor at v3, and move basic custom-component insertion for the whitelisted registry (table, chart, embed, form per §14) into v1 alongside it.

missing: One count. §7's inventory prices `direction.signature-moment` at **10** ('One per direction'); §9.3 prices it at '**2–3 concept candidates**' generated at Step 2 and chosen at Step 4, and adds 'a lint flags a second one'. It is not stated whether the Step-2 prompt should ask for one signature moment per direction or two-to-three candidates within the chosen direction, nor how 10 and 2–3 relate.
why_it_matters: The user's completeness requirement is specifically about per-item variant counts, and this is the item both sections call identity-carrying and Tier A. The number directly shapes the Step-2 prompt template (§6) — asking claude.ai for one concept versus three per direction is a different prompt and a different return schema — and it shapes what the user is shown at Step 4.
suggested_fix: State it once: e.g. Stage A produces one signature-moment concept per direction (10 total), and Stage B produces 2–3 candidate treatments of that concept for the shortlisted direction only. Make §7 and §9.3 quote the same sentence.

missing: A single normative breakpoint set. Four different sets appear: §10.1's switcher offers 390/768/1280/full; §10.8's responsive preflight and §11.8's overflow detector use 320/390/768/1280/1440; §11.4's hard LOCK gate uses 390/768/1440; §11.7 pins four device heights including 1440×900; §11.3 quotes Webflow's 991/767/479 as prior art and §11.4 uses 479 as the demotion boundary. §12.2 additionally says `site.json` records 'breakpoints', implying they are per-project configurable, which no section confirms or denies.
why_it_matters: Two widths (320 and 1440) are gated but not authorable, one (479) is behaviourally significant but appears in no set, and it is unstated whether the user can change any of them. A blocking gate that renders at a width the editor cannot display gives the user a failure they cannot reproduce or fix, which is the worst shape a blocking gate can have.
suggested_fix: Declare one authoring set and one verification set in a single table (e.g. authoring 390/768/1280/full; verification 320/390/479/768/1280/1440), state whether `site.json.breakpoints` is fixed in v1, and make §10.1, §10.8, §11.4, §11.7 and §11.8 all reference it rather than restating widths.

missing: Agreement on how many lock gates exist. §10.8 says 'Four automated gates (§12.5)'; §12.5 lists five and §13 gate 27 refers to 'LOCK purity gates 1–5'.
why_it_matters: Gate 5 is the interaction-manifest check — the one that proves declared motion and interaction behaviour actually exists in the shipped output, i.e. the check that closes the Webflow-export failure class and is the only gate that verifies D4's motion survives LOCK. An implementer working from §10.8's count builds four and drops exactly the gate that protects the motion system.
suggested_fix: Change §10.8 to 'Five automated purity gates (§12.5)' and name gate 5 in the row so it cannot be dropped by miscount.

section: 7 (preamble + variant-count key, applies to every table in 7.1–7.13)
missing: The "Variants" number means three different things in the same tables, and the key defines only one of them. (a) One-value-per-direction: `direction.manifesto` 10, `typeface.display` 10, `grid.personality` 10 — 10 = the number of directions, not options a user chooses between. (b) Option-domain size: `color.neutral-temperature` 4, `density.base-unit` 4, `elevation.model` 5, `cursor.personality` 6 — 10 directions draw values from a domain of 4–6, so several directions must share. (c) Set membership: `color.gradient-set` 6 is six named ROLES (hero wash, card sheen, text gradient, edge fade, radial glow, mesh base) that all ship together; `mark.logo-lockups` 10, `mark.decorative-glyphs` 10, `icon.core-set` ~50 and `shape.clip-and-mask-shapes` 10 are likewise one deliverable set, not N alternatives. The key at §7 only says "A number = distinct pickable options."
why_it_matters: This is the exact requirement the user named ("the components and suggested number of variants of each component"). A builder cannot compute generation volume, cannot size the Step-2 prompt, and cannot decide what control to render: 6 for `color.gradient-set` means "emit six gradients", 6 for `cursor.personality` means "pick one of six". The ambiguity already produced a live contradiction: §7.1 gives `direction.signature-moment` **10**, while §20.1 explicitly EXCLUDES "Ten 'signature moment' variants" in favour of 2–3 bespoke concepts — the two statements only look compatible if you already know the 10 means "one per direction", which the key never says.
suggested_fix: Add a "count kind" column to every §7 table with three legal values — `per-direction` (one value per direction, count = 10 by construction), `domain` (N mutually exclusive options), `set` (N members all delivered) — and restate the variant-count key accordingly. Re-audit all 149 rows against it, and reconcile `direction.signature-moment` with §20.1.

missing: The preamble asserts "A direction is a 26-slot identity vector. Everything else in the system is a pure function of that vector plus shared seed tables." But roughly thirty rows OUTSIDE Category A carry pickable numbers, not `derived`: `type.loading-strategy` 3, `type.numeral-style` 4, `type.emphasis-policy` 6, `type.list-marker-style` 6, `type.quote-treatment` 6, `type.lede-and-dropcap` 5, `layout.aspect-ratio-set` 8, `shape.per-corner-recipes` 8, `shape.stroke-style-set` 4, `shape.divider-treatment` 8, `shape.clip-and-mask-shapes` 10, `effect.backdrop-recipe` 6, `effect.noise-grain` 8, `effect.gradient-mesh` 8, `effect.pattern-tiles` 12, `effect.blend-mode-policy` 6, `color.gradient-set` 6, `color.syntax-highlight` 4, `icon.family-spec` 10, `mark.logo-lockups` 10, `mark.social-share-image` 6, `mark.decorative-glyphs` 10, `color.contrast-ladder` 3, `color.data-vis-categorical` 3, `token.naming-convention` 3, `system.voice-and-microcopy` 10, plus all of 7.9. Nothing states, per row, whether that pick is (i) fixed by the chosen direction, (ii) chosen once site-wide across all directions, or (iii) freely re-pickable by the user inside a chosen direction. Different rows plainly mean different things — `color.contrast-ladder` says "site-level policy chosen once and applied to all directions", `layout.breakpoints` says "shared across all directions", `typeface.display` says one per direction — but `shape.divider-treatment` **8** and `icon.family-spec` **10** say nothing. `token.pick-extension-block` defines `{pickable, slot, directionId, variantIndex, derivedFrom[]}` with no scope field.
why_it_matters: D1 says derived values are computed from the direction and never picked independently, and §20.1 lists "Independent per-item picks for derived values" as excluded, "Enforced structurally via `pickable: false`". If `icon.family-spec` is freely re-pickable inside a direction, a user can put a geometric-mono icon family on an editorial-serif direction and the coherence guarantee D1 exists to provide is gone; if it is fixed by the direction, then it is a 27th identity slot and the vector definition is wrong. The editor literally cannot decide whether to render a control, and the coherence lints in §7.12 cannot be written, because "this direction's scale" is undefined for anything outside the 26 slots.
suggested_fix: Add a `scope` column to every §7 row with values `direction-slot` / `site-global` / `in-direction-repickable`, add the same field to `$extensions['com.acos.pick']`, and state the rule that any `in-direction-repickable` item must have all its options validated against the direction (or be demoted to `direction-slot`). Then either grow the identity vector past 26 or move the genuinely identity-carrying rows (icon family, logo lockup, voice) into Category A.

section: 7.9 and 8 (#Media) vs 6.3 chunking budget and §20.3 U8/U10
missing: No total artwork volume is ever stated, and the two places that imply one disagree by an order of magnitude. §6.3 sizes the whole Step-2/3 hand-carry as "Ten directions plus 20 artworks is ~400KB", matching D1's "20 artworks tagged by direction", and U8's 45–90 minute estimate and U10's ~250-artifact estimate are anchored on that. But §7.9 alone enumerates `art.background-scene` 20 + `art.hero-artwork` 20 + `art.spot-illustrations` 20 + `art.section-divider-shapes` 12 + `art.texture-plates` 12 + `art.photo-grade-recipe` 8 + `art.avatar-style` 8 + `art.3d-or-canvas-scene` 6 + `art.placeholder-strategy` 4 + `art.empty-state` 10 + `art.error-state` 10 = 130 pieces, and §8 (#Media) adds Icon set 20, Illustration set 20, Decorative spot-graphic set 20, Pattern/texture library 20 = 80 more (of which 20 duplicate `art.spot-illustrations`). §20.2 #14 resolves only the pieces-versus-sets axis, not the volume.
why_it_matters: Step 3 is a MANUAL hand-carry the user performs by hand, and §6.4 says clerical load is "the most likely way the product quietly dies". A budget built on 20 artworks that actually has to move ~150–200 artwork artefacts is not off by a rounding error — it invalidates the chunk plan (Chunk "Art" is a single row marked "Variable"), the 45–90 minute estimate, the ~250-artifact payload estimate, and the claim that Stage A is thin. §7.9 also states claude.ai cannot produce raster images, so every one of those pieces must come from Lane A code-drawn art, Lane B ingestion, or a separate Lane C hand-carry — with no per-lane volume split anywhere.
suggested_fix: Add a roll-up table at the end of §7 and §8 giving, per lane (A/B/C) and per phase (v1/v2/v3), the exact artefact count and estimated payload bytes; reconcile it with §6.3's chunk table (add real Art chunk sizing) and re-derive U8/U10 from it. If the true v1 artwork count exceeds what one hand-carry cycle can move, flag the overage for user sign-off rather than leaving §6.3's "20 artworks" standing.

missing: The same artefact carries different variant counts in §7 and §8, with no cross-reference reconciling them: icon families — `icon.family-spec` **10** (§7.8) vs "Icon set **20** … 20 candidate SETS" (§8 Media); logo lockups — `mark.logo-lockups` **10** (§7.8) vs "Logo lockup set **6** — the standard brand deliverable set" (§8 Media); social/OG images — `mark.social-share-image` **6** (§7.8) vs "OG / social share card template **3**" (§8 Utility); section seams — `shape.divider-treatment` **8** (§7.6) vs `art.section-divider-shapes` **12** (§7.9) vs "Section divider / seam **10**" (§8 Content); patterns — `effect.pattern-tiles` **12** (§7.6) vs `art.texture-plates` **12** (§7.9) vs "Pattern / texture library **20**" (§8 Media); photography — `imagery.treatment` **10** (§7.1, an identity slot) vs `art.photo-grade-recipe` **8** (§7.9) vs "Photography treatment **8**" (§8 Media); empty/error art — `art.empty-state` **10** / `art.error-state` **10** (§7.9) vs "Empty state **8**" / "Error state **6**" / "404 **6**" / "500 **3**" (§8).
